name: Harare
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Harare: sanctions-aware due diligence, gold trade reviews and asset research in Zimbabwe's capital.
hero_lede: Harare is Zimbabwe's capital and its financial, commercial and communications hub, where mining, tobacco and agricultural trade, banking and government contracting are concentrated. TDSC scopes sanctions-aware investigative consulting for matters touching the city from Nashville, coordinating Zimbabwean counsel and qualified local professionals where needed.
intro: Harare is Zimbabwe's capital and largest city. The 2022 census counted 1,849,600 people in the City of Harare and 2,427,209 in Harare Province, about 16 percent of the national population, with Greater Harare, including Chitungwiza, Epworth, Ruwa and Norton, at roughly 2.61 million. The city is the country's main financial, commercial and communications centre and a trading centre for tobacco, maize, cotton and citrus. Manufacturing of textiles, steel and chemicals and trade in gold, diamonds and platinum are economically significant, and Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport, the country's largest, connects Harare with Johannesburg and the wider region.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Harare because ownership and control of Zimbabwe's mining, fuel, agriculture and infrastructure businesses are concentrated there, often close to the state. In March 2024 the United States ended its Zimbabwe sanctions programme but designated the President, senior security officials and a prominent businessman's network, including Sakunda Holdings, under the Global Magnitsky programme for corruption and human rights abuses. Companies dealing with Zimbabwean counterparties therefore need to know who owns them, how they won contracts or licences, and whether they connect to designated persons or to the gold and diamond smuggling networks described by US authorities.

matters.title: Sanctions-linked ownership screening
matters.text: Since March 2024, US designations have focused on the President, security officials and a business network including Sakunda Holdings and Fossil entities. Before any transaction, Harare counterparties are screened for ownership or control links to designated persons, which often requires reconstructing group structures beyond a simple list check.

matters.title: Gold and minerals trade reviews
matters.text: Harare is the commercial centre for Zimbabwe's trade in gold, diamonds and platinum. Buyers, refiners and financiers review exporters, intermediaries and offtake partners for ownership, licensing, provenance and links to the smuggling networks that US authorities have publicly described.

matters.title: Government contract counterparties
matters.text: Fuel supply, infrastructure, energy and agricultural input contracts are negotiated with ministries and state entities in Harare. Reviews of local partners and suppliers examine political connections, procurement history, performance on earlier contracts and allegations reported in Zimbabwean press.

matters.title: Tobacco and agribusiness counterparties
matters.text: Harare is a trading centre for tobacco, maize, cotton and citrus. Merchants, contractors and lenders review buyers, contractors and processors for ownership, financial strength, side-marketing disputes and payment history before extending credit or entering supply arrangements.

matters.title: Asset tracing and recovery
matters.text: Creditors with claims against Zimbabwean parties need to identify property, company interests and accounts, much of it held in Harare and sometimes moved into South Africa or offshore. Work maps holdings and transfers lawfully and helps counsel assess enforcement prospects in Zimbabwe and abroad.

local_context.title: Courts sitting in Harare
local_context.text: Harare is the seat of the Constitutional Court, Supreme Court and the main station of the High Court, where most significant commercial litigation is heard. The High Court in Harare has a specialised commercial division intended to speed up business disputes. Judgments published by the courts and reported in Zimbabwean press are a primary source on litigation involving Harare companies and their owners, although online coverage is uneven and court file searches usually require local counsel.

local_context.title: US sanctions position since 2024
local_context.text: On 4 March 2024 the United States terminated the Zimbabwe Sanctions Regulations and removed persons designated solely under that programme, then designated 11 individuals and three entities, Sakunda Holdings, Fossil Agro and Fossil Contracting, under Global Magnitsky authorities. Advisers have noted that companies should continue to review transactions involving Zimbabwean government entities and officials carefully. Other jurisdictions' measures should be checked separately for each matter.

local_context.title: Company records and regulators
local_context.text: The Registrar of Companies, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe and the main financial and mining regulators are based in Harare. National company and beneficial ownership disclosure rules are covered on our Zimbabwe page; in practice, Harare-based groups often hold assets through layered private companies and trusts, and registry data must be combined with court records, regulator notices, gazette publications and press archives to reconstruct control.

local_context.title: Local reporting and public sources
local_context.text: Harare is home to the country's main newspapers, including state-owned and independent titles, which often report on procurement, mining deals and business disputes from different perspectives. Using both, alongside regional South African coverage and international investigative reporting, helps establish a balanced public record on Harare companies and individuals whose reputations are politically contested. Reports cite each source so readers can weigh it.

tdsc_approach: For Harare matters TDSC begins with sanctions screening. As a US company, it screens every party, owner and transaction flow against current US and other applicable sanctions, including the Global Magnitsky designations of March 2024, and does not accept engagements that would violate them. Research then maps ownership and control using registry information available through lawful channels, court judgments, regulator and gazette notices, and both state-owned and independent Zimbabwean press, alongside regional sources. Where interviews, site visits or retrieval of court and property documents are needed, TDSC coordinates qualified Zimbabwean professionals under the direction of the client's Zimbabwean counsel. Sources and contacts are handled with particular care given the political sensitivity of many Harare matters.

faqs.q: Is Zimbabwe still under US sanctions?
faqs.a: The country-specific Zimbabwe sanctions programme was terminated on 4 March 2024. On the same day the United States designated the President, other senior officials, a businessman and three entities, including Sakunda Holdings, under Global Magnitsky authorities. Dealings with those persons and entities they control remain prohibited for US persons, so screening is still essential.

faqs.q: Why is ownership research so important for Harare counterparties?
faqs.a: Major businesses in fuel, mining, agriculture and infrastructure are often held through private companies whose ultimate owners are not obvious, and some have political connections. A list check alone may miss ownership or control by a designated person, so reconstructing the group structure is often the core of a Harare engagement.

faqs.q: Where are commercial disputes heard in Harare?
faqs.a: Most significant commercial cases are heard at the High Court in Harare, which has a commercial division for business disputes. Appeals go to the Supreme Court, also in Harare. Many international contracts with Zimbabwean parties provide for arbitration, often seated outside Zimbabwe. Court file searches in Harare generally require local counsel.

faqs.q: Can TDSC review gold or mineral suppliers based in Harare?
faqs.a: Yes. TDSC researches the supplier's ownership, licensing, sources of material, banking and reputation using lawful public sources and qualified local contacts, and screens for links to sanctioned persons and smuggling allegations. It does not access restricted government systems, and reports state clearly where provenance cannot be documented.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office in Harare?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is based in Nashville, Tennessee and has no office or staff in Zimbabwe. Engagements touching Harare are scoped and managed from Nashville after sanctions screening. Where local work is required, TDSC coordinates qualified Zimbabwean professionals and works with the client's Zimbabwean counsel. Field work is never presented as TDSC's own.
